strengths: Introduces NeuroBuds, an earphone-based ExG sensing prototype, and DailySense, a new dataset with 50 hours of free-living ExG data plus 20 hours of labeled data spanning five human senses, addressing the lack of diverse real-world ExG data.

Proposes Physiology-informed Multi-band Tokenization (PiMT), a clear and intuitive tokenization scheme that decomposes ExG signals into 12 physiological sub-bands and combines it with a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder and reconstruction-based pretraining.

Evaluates on six DailySense tasks and four public ExG benchmarks, with additional analyses on pretraining data scale, band count, patch size, backbone choice, LOSO, cross-session/cross-subject generalization, and smartphone efficiency.
Shows that multi-band tokenization improves over fewer-band variants, and that pretraining on free-living data yields substantial gains on DailySense compared with the selected PatchTST baseline.
The paper is generally well written, and the filter-bank design is described clearly enough to be partially reproducible.
weaknesses: The main DailySense evaluation uses an 8:2 random split per participant over 4-second windows, which likely leaks highly correlated adjacent/same-session windows into training and testing. The resulting within-session numbers are much higher than the cross-subject results in Appendix L, where PiMT barely outperforms PatchTST (58.6 vs. 58.0 average F1). This undermines the central claim of task-agnostic real-world generalization.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and potentially unfair. On public benchmarks, only PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba are compared, while relevant ExG foundation models (e.g., BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM) and standard EEG models (EEGNet, EEGConformer, DeepConvNet) are omitted. It is also unclear whether the public-benchmark baselines receive the same free-living pretraining as PiMT, which would confound the comparison.

The multi-band tokenization contribution is incremental and its physiological grounding is weak. The 12 bands overlap heavily, several are non-standard or arbitrarily narrow (e.g., EMG-High 95-100 Hz, ECG-HF 0.12-0.488 Hz), and no comparison is made to learnable filter banks, wavelets, random filters, or standard EEG bands. The claim of 12 distinct physiological modalities is overstated.

The pretraining ablation does not support the claimed complementary benefits of the six reconstruction tasks. Full performance is 0.876 average F1, while removing individual components gives 0.871-0.873, with some ablated variants even better on gaze or video. Differences are within noise and no significance tests are reported.

DailySense task-specific data are small (up to seven participants per task) and many tasks are subjective or physiologically surprising (interest inference, taste, smell). The paper provides no rigorous validation that the ear-based device captures reliable EEG/EMG/EOG/ECG signals compared with standard equipment, and the gaze error around 6 degrees is not compelling for practical gaze tracking.

Reproducibility and consistency issues remain: it is unclear whether DailySense or code will be released, hardware replication is nontrivial, and the text contains inconsistencies such as 50 vs. 40 hours of free-living data, 3.1% vs. 3.6% memory usage, and 6.15 vs. 6.11 degree gaze error.

The public-benchmark transfer setting is questionable. Pretraining on ear-based free-living ExG and then fine-tuning on head-EEG datasets such as SEED, DREAMER, Sleep-EDF, and BCI IV 2b introduces substantial domain shift, but no analysis or controls are provided to show that the gains come from the proposed representation rather than from extra data or fine-tuning details.

The paper overclaims state-of-the-art, foundation-model, and task-agnostic status. The model is small (e.g., hidden dimension 16, embedding dimension 64), pretraining is limited to roughly 50 hours, and the empirical gains over strong baselines are often modest or within standard deviation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable, task-agnostic ExG representation learning from wearable earphone-based sensing, with a clear motivation around data diversity and task-specific frequency-band limitations.

The hardware and dataset effort are substantial: NeuroBuds and DailySense provide 70 hours of ear-ExG recordings, including free-living data and task-specific data across five human senses, which could be valuable if properly released and validated.

The proposed PiMT pipeline is coherent and well motivated: physiology-informed multi-band filtering, patch tokenization, a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder, and reconstruction-based self-supervised pretraining.
The experimental section covers both the new DailySense benchmark and four public ExG datasets, with ablations on number of frequency bands, pretraining components, patch size, and backbone choice.
The paper includes an ethics statement, reproducibility statement, and appendices with hardware, data collection, and hyperparameter details, which helps clarify some implementation choices.
If the dataset and evaluation were made rigorous, the work could have impact on wearable physiological sensing and foundation models for ExG.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: fixed physiology-inspired filter banks, multi-band tokenization, reconstruction-based SSL, and Mamba/Transformer encoders are all well-established components; the contribution reads more like a sensible engineering combination than a new AI method.

The evaluation appears to suffer from serious data leakage. DailySense and public benchmark results are based on random 80/20 splits of 4-second windows, often within the same session/subject, while labels are repeated over many windows from the same trial or stimulus. This inflates F1 scores and does not measure generalization.

The cross-subject/cross-session results contradict the main claims. Appendix Table 7 shows PiMT cross-subject average F1 of only 0.586 versus 0.876 within-session, and gaze error is worse than PatchTST (7.78° vs 7.07°), yet the main text claims effective generalization to unseen users.

The DailySense tasks are weakly designed. 'Interest inference' assigns clip-level labels to 4-second windows, and taste/smell/touch tasks may be confounded by facial EMG, mouth/nose movements, and other artifacts rather than sensory or cognitive processing. No artifact-control experiments are provided.

State-of-the-art claims are unsupported. On public benchmarks, the paper compares only against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba, omitting strong ExG-specific and foundation-model baselines such as EEGConformer, BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM, and others. Reported BCI IV 2b F1 (0.693), SEED F1 (0.820), and Sleep-EDF F1 (0.822) are not clearly state-of-the-art.

The pretraining ablation undermines the proposed six reconstruction objectives. Removing any single component changes average F1 only from 0.876 to 0.871-0.873, all within standard deviation, so the claimed complementary benefits are not demonstrated.

The multi-band ablation does not control for sequence length or model capacity. Increasing from 1 to 12 bands increases the number of tokens and computation substantially, so the performance gain may reflect greater capacity rather than physiological multi-band decomposition.

Important implementation details are inconsistent: the pretraining corpus is described as 50 hours in the main text but 40 hours in Appendix G; the Mamba backbone is described as 8 layers in Appendix F and 16 layers in Appendix G; gaze error is called MSE in the text but reported as mean angular error.

Reproducibility is limited. No code or dataset link is provided, and DailySense availability is not stated, despite the dataset being a central contribution. The hardware description is insufficient to fully reproduce the sensing platform.

Gaze tracking performance is not practically compelling: roughly 6° mean angular error is far worse than commodity eye trackers and only marginally better than baselines, so the claim of accurate gaze tracking is overstated.

The paper lacks statistical significance testing, and many reported improvements are within noise given the large standard deviations. The LOSO claim of performance 'comparable to full pretraining' is also inconsistent with the cross-subject results.

strengths: Introduces NeuroBuds, a low-cost earphone-based ExG sensing prototype, and DailySense, a 70-hour dataset with 50h free-living and 20h labeled recordings across five human senses, which is a valuable resource for wearable ExG research.

Proposes PiMT, a physiology-informed multi-band tokenization scheme using 12 canonical sub-bands, a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder, and reconstruction-based pretraining; the approach is reasonable, well-motivated, and clearly described.
Reports extensive experiments: DailySense tasks, four public benchmarks, ablations, saliency analysis, data-scaling curves, LOSO/cross-session evaluation, and on-device efficiency analysis.
Addresses an important and under-explored problem: task-agnostic ExG representation learning outside controlled lab settings, with potential impact on wearable physiological sensing.
The manuscript is generally well-written, and the appendices provide useful hardware, protocol, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The public benchmark evaluation uses a random 80/20 split after shuffling 4-second windows, which likely causes subject/session leakage and substantially overestimates performance; this undermines the claimed generalization and state-of-the-art results on DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, and BCI IV 2b.

Table 2 compares only PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba, omitting standard ExG baselines (EEGNet, DeepConvNet, EEGConformer, TST) and discussed ExG foundation models (BIOT, BrainWave, BrainBERT), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not supported.

Cross-subject results in Table 7 show PiMT barely outperforming PatchTST on average (0.586 vs. 0.580) and performing worse on gaze (7.78° vs. 7.07°), contradicting the paper's strong generalization claims.

The main DailySense evaluation appears to use within-session random splits, while cross-user and cross-session performance is much lower; participant counts per task are small (up to 7), raising concerns about real-world generalization and label reliability.

There is no ablation of a pretrained Bidirectional-Mamba without multi-band tokenization, so gains may be confounded by the backbone, pretraining, and tokenization; the component ablations in Table 4 show differences largely within noise.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or DailySense dataset release plan is stated, hardware signal quality is not quantitatively validated against standard electrodes, and hyperparameters are inconsistent (e.g., 8 vs. 16 layers).

Some technical concerns remain: the 12 filter bands overlap and are somewhat arbitrary, 4-second windows cannot resolve sub-0.25 Hz ECG bands, there are notation/typo errors (e.g., 'PiFT', duplicated frequency-reconstruction equations), and ~6° gaze error is high for practical gaze tracking.

Ethical and privacy considerations for free-living physiological data are under-addressed beyond a brief IRB statement, especially regarding consent, data sharing, and potential inference of sensitive health information.

strengths: Introduces NeuroBuds, a low-cost earphone-based ExG sensing prototype, and DailySense, a new dataset with 50h free-living and 20h labeled data spanning five human senses. This is a valuable data-collection and benchmark contribution.

Proposes PiMT, a physiology-informed multi-band tokenization scheme that decomposes ExG into 12 canonical frequency bands and uses a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder with reconstruction-based pre-training. The idea is reasonable and avoids task-specific filtering.

Evaluation is broad in scope: DailySense with six tasks plus four public benchmarks, multiple baselines, ablations on tokenization/pre-training/patch size, saliency analysis, data-scale study, LOSO, on-device latency, and significance testing.
Shows consistent gains over several baselines on DailySense and improvements on public benchmarks, and demonstrates that free-living pre-training can help transfer.
weaknesses: Main DailySense evaluation uses an 80/20 random split of 4-second windows within each participant/session, so train and test windows often come from the same recording session and even the same stimulus clip. This can inflate performance and does not support claims of task-agnostic or real-world generalization. The more rigorous cross-subject result drops to ~58.6% average F1, near chance for binary tasks, and gaze error is worse than PatchTST in that setting.

The paper positions itself as an ExG foundation model but does not compare against state-of-the-art ExG self-supervised/foundation models such as BIOT, BrainBERT, LaBraM, BrainWave, or Neuro-GPT. The main public-benchmark table compares only to PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba; under the standardized EEGConformer preprocessing, EEGConformer is already competitive, so SOTA claims are not well supported.

The 12-band filter bank is not clearly principled or task-agnostic: bands overlap heavily (e.g., EEG-gamma 30-100 Hz, EMG-LF 15-45 Hz, EMG-mid 45-95 Hz, QRS 8-50 Hz), and ECG bands are included even though the earphone hardware is not shown to reliably capture ECG. There is no leave-one-band-out analysis, learned filter bank comparison, or justification for the exact band definitions.

Pre-training ablations are weak: removing individual reconstruction tasks changes average F1 by only 0.003-0.005, and some removals improve individual tasks (e.g., w/o P improves Video F1 from 0.964 to 0.979; w/o A improves Taste from 0.801 to 0.816). The claim that all six components are complementary is not strongly supported.

Dataset scale and diversity are limited: 22 participants, with only up to seven participants per labeled task, and limited demographic information. This is small for foundation-model pre-training and raises questions about the generality of the learned representations. There is also no clear statement or link for public release of the dataset, code, or hardware design, limiting reproducibility.

Evaluation details and metrics are inconsistent: gaze is described as MSE in Section 5.1 but reported as angular error/MAE in tables; ~6° error is coarse for many gaze applications. Public benchmark splits appear to be random 80/20, which may not follow standard cross-subject/cross-session protocols and can be overoptimistic.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art' is not supported in cross-subject settings (PiMT is only 0.586 vs. 0.580 F1 and worse gaze than PatchTST), and public benchmark gains over PatchTST are small (e.g., Sleep-EDF 0.810 to 0.822, BCI IV 2b 0.657 to 0.693).

Ethical/privacy considerations for continuous earphone-based physiological monitoring are under-addressed; the ethics statement only notes IRB approval and asserts no ethical issue, without discussing data privacy, consent for release, or potential misuse.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: building generalizable ExG representations for real-world, wearable sensing beyond lab-controlled settings.
It integrates hardware (NeuroBuds), a new dataset (DailySense), and a representation-learning method (PiMT), which is an ambitious and potentially impactful combination.
DailySense, with 50 hours of free-living ear-ExG and 20 hours of labeled task data across multiple tasks, could be a valuable resource if properly validated and released.
PiMT is a reasonable engineering combination of physiology-informed multi-band decomposition, patch tokenization, reconstruction-based pretraining, and a Mamba encoder.
The experimental section is extensive, including multiple datasets, ablations, statistical tests, efficiency analysis, and cross-condition evaluations.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is likely to leak information. DailySense results use random 8:2 splits of 4-second windows from the same participants, sessions, and often the same trials. For video/audio interest, clip-level ratings appear to be assigned to all windows in a clip, making the task closer to clip identification than per-window physiological inference. This inflates the reported F1 scores and undermines the central claims.

Generalization claims are contradicted by the paper's own cross-subject and cross-session results. In Appendix O, PiMT is not better than PatchTST under cross-subject evaluation (0.586 vs. 0.580 average F1) and has worse gaze error (7.78° vs. 7.07°). The main claims of task-agnostic and in-the-wild generalization are therefore not supported.

The five-senses tasks are confounded by EMG/EOG artifacts. Taste, smell, and touch involve sipping, sniffing, rubbing, and facial movements, all of which produce strong peri-auricular muscle signals. The saliency analysis even attributes high-frequency activation to peri-auricular EMG, but no control analyses rule out artifact-based classification. The model may be detecting motor/expression patterns rather than sensory or cognitive processing.

The public benchmark evaluation is inconsistent and incomplete. Table 2 reports SEED F1 = 0.820 and BCI IV 2b F1 = 0.693, while Appendix Table 5 reports much higher values (0.971 and 0.869) under what is described as the EEGConformer preprocessing pipeline. Section 5.1 claims public benchmarks follow the official EEGConformer implementation, yet EEGConformer itself is omitted from the main public benchmark table. This makes the state-of-the-art claim unclear and undermines reproducibility.

The paper claims state-of-the-art performance but compares only against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba on public benchmarks. It omits strong ExG self-supervised/foundation-model baselines such as BIOT, BrainBERT, BrainWave, and EEGConformer in the main comparison. On DailySense, only PatchTST receives a pretraining comparison, while other baselines are not pretrained on the same free-living data.

The novelty of PiMT is incremental. It combines a fixed filter bank of standard physiological bands, patch tokenization, masked reconstruction, and a Mamba encoder. Several bands overlap heavily (e.g., EEG-gamma 30–100 Hz, EMG-LF 15–45 Hz, EMG-mid 45–95 Hz, QRS 8–50 Hz), creating redundant tokens. The 12-band gain over 4-band is modest and may simply reflect more tokens/compute; no control for sequence length or parameter count is provided.

The pretraining ablation does not convincingly support the claimed complementary benefits. Removing any single reconstruction component changes average F1 only from 0.876 to 0.871–0.873, and some gaze errors are lower without components (e.g., w/o P: 5.98° vs. full: 6.00°). This suggests the six-task pretraining design is not well justified.

Dataset and hardware validation are limited. NeuroBuds is compared to OpenBCI on only two participants and about one hour of data, with an average correlation of 0.71. There is no detailed signal-quality, SNR, artifact, or electrode-placement validation. The dataset is not clearly released, and no code/data availability statement is provided, limiting reproducibility and impact.

The 'five human senses' and 'task-agnostic' framing is overstated. Interest inference is not a sensory modality, and taste/smell classification from earphone electrodes is not shown to reflect neural sensory processing. The model is still fine-tuned with task-specific heads for each downstream task, so it is not task-agnostic at inference time.

Statistical significance testing treats participant-seed pairs as independent, ignoring within-participant correlation across seeds and tasks. The extremely small p-values are therefore likely inflated, and no multiple-comparison correction is applied.

Ethical and privacy considerations are under-discussed. The system performs emotion/interest inference and collects physiological data from human participants, but the paper only states IRB approval and does not address data release, consent, privacy, or potential misuse of continuous physiological monitoring.

strengths: Introduces NeuroBuds, an earphone-based ExG sensing prototype, and DailySense, a new dataset with 50 hours of free-living and 20 hours of task-specific recordings across five human senses, addressing data diversity and real-world ExG monitoring.

Proposes PiMT, a physiology-informed multi-band tokenization scheme with a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder and reconstruction-based pretraining, which is well motivated and integrates hardware, dataset, and model design.

Extensive experiments on DailySense and four public benchmarks, including ablations over frequency bands, pretraining components, tokenization strategies, patch size, frozen encoders, data scale, efficiency, and statistical significance tests.
Reports strong DailySense results with pretraining (87.6% average F1) and consistent improvements over several baselines, with additional LOSO and cross-session analyses.
The hardware-dataset-algorithm co-design has potential impact for wearable ExG foundation models and free-living physiological sensing.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: multi-band filtering, patch tokenization, Mamba, and reconstruction objectives are existing components; the main novelty is the specific band bank and the hardware/dataset contribution.

Public benchmark evaluation is incomplete and inconsistent: main Table 2 compares only PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba, omitting ExG foundation models and EEGConformer, while Appendix Table 5 reports much higher and very different SEED/BCI numbers, making state-of-the-art claims unclear.

Main DailySense results use random 80/20 window-level splits, which can leak temporal and subject information; cross-subject performance drops to 58.6% F1 and gaze error is worse than PatchTST, contradicting strong generalization claims.
Reproducibility is limited: no clear data or code release/access protocol is stated, and the reproducibility statement only covers filter-bank details, which weakens the benchmark contribution.
The 12-band filter bank contains overlapping and redundant bands (e.g., EOG 0.1–20 Hz overlaps EEG bands, EMG overlaps EEG, ECG/QRS bands), and the 12-band gains are modest on several tasks.

Pretraining component ablations show only small differences (0.871–0.876), with some ablated variants outperforming the full model on individual tasks, so the claimed complementarity is not strongly supported.

Gaze tracking error (~6°) is not clearly state-of-the-art, and hardware validation is limited to two participants with OpenBCI correlation, leaving signal quality and practical utility not fully established.
